source.title: Robust Learning at Noisy Labeled Medical Images: Applied to Skin Lesion Classification
source.authors: Cheng Xue; Q. Dou; Xueying Shi; Hao Chen; Pheng-Ann Heng

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Tests fitting and generalization under partially corrupted labels on medical images, using a pretrained ResNet-101 and a noise-selection procedure different from the original studies’ random-label experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper tests 5%, 10%, 20% and 40% corrupted labels, not a completely random labeling. Table 1 reports clean-test accuracy for the ResNet baseline; the text describes training error and learning-time trends from Fig. 3 without numeric values. The cited findings from Zhang et al. and Arpit et al. are not extracted as this paper’s results.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own baseline ResNet-101 memorization, convergence and generalization results in medical-image classification. These bear on V2, V4 and V6, although corruption targets high-loss images rather than uniformly random examples.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors report that ResNet can memorize corrupted medical-image labels and requires more epochs at higher corruption. Their main conclusion is that uncertainty-based sample selection plus individual reweighting improves noisy-label classification without pre-estimating the noise distribution or requiring extra clean data.
record.recipe_differences: Uses partially corrupted medical-image labels on an ImageNet-initialized ResNet-101; the paper studies noisy-label fitting rather than fitting fully random labels in the original settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported training behavior varies with the corrupted-label percentage: more noise requires more epochs, and clean-test accuracy declines as the noise ratio increases.
record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Symposium on Biomedical Imaging
record.problems: The noisy-label ratios stop at 40%, not complete random labeling. Training-error and epoch trends are qualitative and lack numeric values or uncertainty estimates. Table 1 reports accuracy, not test error, and does not state uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 also reports Panini, ResNet+OUSM and Our method for the 5%–40% noise conditions. Those results compare noise-handling methods rather than the standard ResNet baseline central to the claim, so they are not included as claim rows.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, near-zero training error under that condition, chance test performance and unchanged training settings.
Small constant-factor training cost relative to true labels and timing under completely random labeling.
Uniformly random corruption, corruption above 40%, the chance endpoint and zero training error at 0% corruption. Training-error and Table 1 accuracy results use different learning rates.
Regularization ablations, prevention of completely random-label fitting and generalization after removing regularization.
Separate clean-versus-corrupted example learning curves and learning dynamics under fully random labels.

missing.what: The clean-label ResNet baseline achieves 86.3% test accuracy, completing the reported 0%, 5%, 10%, 20%, 40% accuracy sequence.
missing.locator: Section 3.3 and Table 1, ResNet row, 0% column

record.verdict_notes: The corruption procedure selects high-loss examples within each class and flips their binary labels; it does not establish uniformly random label assignment. Its description also contains inconsistent sample totals. The statement that test error decreases with greater corruption conflicts with Table 1's declining accuracy and should not be treated as evidence of improved generalization.

versions.untested_parts: No completely random labeling of the full training set; the study tests only 5%–40% corrupted labels.
The paper says more epochs are needed as noise increases, but does not quantify a small constant-factor time cost.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel or Gaussian-noise inputs.
No 100% corruption condition; the reported ratios are 5%, 10%, 20% and 40%, with no 0% training-curve condition.
No test of whether weight decay, dropout or data augmentation prevent fitting random labels, or whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
The paper reports a qualitative learning-order observation for partially noisy labels; it does not test fully random labels or separately quantify learning of real and noisy labels over time.

rows.subject: ResNet-101 initialized with Imagenet weight
rows.operation_detail: Compared learning curves as the noisy-label percentage increased; authors report that more epochs were needed to fit all training data.
rows.measure: Epochs needed to fit all training data
rows.baseline: fewer epochs at lower noise percentage
rows.value: need more epochs as the noise percentage increases
rows.note: The time increase is qualitative; no epoch counts or constant-factor comparison are reported.
rows.check: Supports only slower convergence with increasing corruption. No epoch counts, runtime ratios or clean-label timing comparison establish a small constant-factor cost.

rows.subject: ResNet-101 initialized with Imagenet weight
rows.operation_detail: Observed validation accuracy during training on datasets with noisy labels; authors state that simple patterns are learned before memorizing noise.
rows.measure: Learning order of simple patterns and noisy labels
rows.value: Validation accuracy decreases through training as DNNs learn simple patterns first before memorizing the noise.
rows.note: The paper attributes the learning-order statement to the validation-accuracy trend and cites Arpit et al. [13].
rows.check: This is the authors' interpretation of declining held-out accuracy, with an Arpit citation; clean and corrupted examples' learning trajectories are not separately measured. The text ambiguously calls the held-out set validation data, while Fig. 3 names official test data.
